article_blocks.text: Strain Type: Indica-dominant hybrid
Genetics: Warlock × Northern Lights × White Widow
Breeder: Magus Genetics
THC Content: 18%–24%
CBD Content: Low
Terpene Profile: pinene , myrcene , caryophyllene
Primary Flavors: Sweet pine, earth, resin, spice, subtle fruit
Flowering Time (Indoor): 60–67 days
Outdoor Harvest Time: October into November
Indoor Yield: 400–500 g/m²
Outdoor Yield: Moderate
Grow Difficulty: Moderate

Exile belongs to a nearly vanished chapter of Dutch cannabis breeding. Rather than being another contemporary marijuana cultivar assembled from Cookies, Gelato or modern dessert genetics, it was created during the period when Northern Lights, White Widow, Skunk and Afghan-derived lines formed the backbone of European seed breeding. Gerrit of Magus Genetics combined his celebrated Warlock with a Northern Lights × White Widow female to build an indica-dominant weed strain with greater physical weight, heavier production and an unmistakably sweet pine aroma. The finished hybrid contained approximately 50% Warlock, 25% Northern Lights and 25% White Widow, giving it a genetic composition that reads almost like a collection of influential 1990s cannabis history.

Its story is also different from most surviving classic strains . Serious Seeds eventually acquired the Magus Genetics collection and preserved several of Gerrit’s creations, including Warlock, Double Dutch , Biddy Early and Motavation . Exile could not be saved. According to Serious Seeds’ own history, the original mother plant had already been lost, making the authentic seed line unavailable from the company today. That loss has helped turn Exile into something of a historical cultivar rather than a widely circulating dispensary strain. Old breeder material nevertheless provides a detailed picture of what it was supposed to be: a compact, dark-leaved marijuana plant carrying a strong sweet-pine scent and finishing with a powerful, deeply physical stone.
Genetics and Lineage

Exile’s pedigree is best written as Warlock × (Northern Lights × White Widow). Magus Genetics described the genetic balance more specifically as 50% Warlock, 25% Northern Lights and 25% White Widow. Warlock was Gerrit’s foundational breeding achievement, developed from Skunk and Afghani material after years of selection. Serious Seeds records that the same Warlock breeding stock later became the father behind several Magus projects, including Exile. The choice of Warlock was significant because it already combined an indica-shaped plant with a surprisingly strong cerebral component, substantial flower formation and a sweet aromatic character.

Northern Lights moved the cross further toward the indica side. Its reputation for compact architecture, resin production and a tranquil body-oriented effect complemented Warlock without introducing excessive flowering stretch. White Widow contributed another layer of resin potential along with hybrid vigor and greater aromatic complexity. Instead of producing a simple three-strain blend in which every ancestor was equally obvious, Gerrit’s selection remained strongly Warlock-influenced. Historical descriptions note that Exile grew much like its Warlock parent but stretched less after the photoperiod changed, developed larger dark-green leaves and required roughly an additional week to finish.

That genetic structure explains why surviving descriptions sometimes disagree about the exact indica-to-sativa ratio. Percentages such as 70/30 or 75/25 are estimates rather than a meaningful breeder specification. What matters horticulturally is that the plant behaves as an indica-dominant hybrid while retaining some of the mental character associated with Warlock and White Widow. For an old-school cannabis collector, the pedigree is especially notable because it brings together four enormously influential families once the Skunk and Afghan ancestry behind Warlock is considered.
Effects and Experience

The experience begins with considerable potency but generally develops differently from a bright, energetic sativa. Early effects can produce a noticeable mental shift, easing attention away from outside distractions and giving the strain the inward-looking quality that helped inspire its name. Rather than generating rapid stimulation, Exile tends to narrow the field of attention. Thoughts may become slower, music more absorbing and physical surroundings less demanding. That inward transition can feel euphoric in moderate amounts, although the cultivar was never primarily marketed as a daytime productivity strain.

Its second phase is where the indica character becomes unmistakable. Muscular tension can gradually diminish while the limbs feel heavier and physical activity becomes less appealing. Historical Magus material characterized the effect as powerful and primarily bodily, with a sedative quality that distinguished Exile from the more head-oriented Warlock. The combination of Northern Lights and White Widow further reinforces that depth, producing marijuana better suited to a quiet evening than a demanding schedule. Higher doses may progress into pronounced drowsiness, particularly for consumers without a strong THC tolerance.

Potency figures attached to Exile today vary widely, partly because the original breeding population is no longer commercially maintained. Modern references sometimes place samples in the upper teens or low-to-mid 20% THC range, but those numbers should not be interpreted as a guaranteed characteristic of historical Magus seed stock. Individual response also depends on far more than percentage alone. Dose, tolerance, cannabinoid composition and terpene expression can all change the experience, and excessive THC may produce dizziness, anxiety, impaired coordination or an uncomfortable degree of sedation.
Medical Benefits

Exile’s deeply relaxing character made it attractive to medical marijuana consumers long before strain descriptions routinely included lists of possible therapeutic applications. A body-heavy THC effect may appeal to some adults dealing with persistent discomfort, physical tension or an inability to settle down at night. Sedating cannabis may also be chosen by patients who find more stimulating varieties counterproductive when rest is the objective. Appetite enhancement and mood elevation are additional effects sometimes associated with strong indica-dominant marijuana.

There is an important distinction between those practical uses and established medical evidence. No clinical research has demonstrated that Exile itself treats a particular disease, and strain names are not standardized pharmaceutical formulations. Research into cannabis and cannabinoids provides some evidence for benefit in certain chronic pain settings, but results depend on cannabinoid composition, dose and medical context rather than the commercial name printed on a container. Anyone considering cannabis for a medical condition should therefore treat the cultivar’s effect profile as descriptive information, not as proof of treatment efficacy.

Its comparatively sedating character also creates limitations. Weed that produces heavy physical relaxation may interfere with driving, work, coordination and other activities requiring alertness. Cannabis can additionally interact with medications, while THC may worsen anxiety or other symptoms in susceptible individuals. For patients, the most useful information is the tested cannabinoid content of the actual product being consumed rather than historical expectations associated with the Exile name.
Flavor Profile and Aroma

Fresh Exile plants earned a reputation for an aroma that could become surprisingly aggressive during flowering. Sweetness forms the foundation, but pine pushes strongly through the bouquet, producing a scent closer to resinous evergreen branches than the candy-like profiles found in many newer hybrids. Behind the pine are damp earth, old-school hash, woody spice and a faint fruitiness inherited from Warlock. Historical descriptions specifically emphasize that the sharp smell of the living plant becomes more pleasant after drying and curing, when the individual elements settle into a smoother composition.

The taste follows the same general direction. Pine and sweet resin tend to arrive first, followed by earthy marijuana flavors and a lightly spicy finish. Some expressions may carry more fruit, while others emphasize the darker Afghan and Northern Lights side of the family. Because no authoritative terpene laboratory profile exists for the original Magus population, exact terpene rankings should be treated cautiously. The strong evergreen aroma strongly suggests an important pinene contribution, while myrcene and beta-caryophyllene would be consistent with its earthy, herbal and peppery dimensions, but individual surviving plants may differ substantially.

What separates Exile from many modern marijuana strains is the absence of an exaggerated dessert theme. There is no need to search for artificial-sounding notes of frosting, candy or tropical syrup to understand the appeal. Its aroma belongs firmly to an older cannabis vocabulary: pine forest, resin, earth, sweetness and spice. A careful cure is particularly important because the fresh flowers can smell considerably sharper than the finished weed.
Growing Information

Exile was designed primarily with indoor cultivation in mind. The plant grows with a sturdy, predominantly indica architecture, producing large dark-green leaves and relatively manageable internodal spacing. Compared with Warlock, it tends to stretch less when flowering begins. Branches develop strongly enough to support a productive canopy, and historical cultivation references describe the strain as adaptable to conventional indoor systems. Magus material placed flowering at approximately 60–67 days, equivalent to roughly nine or ten weeks, while period reference material records potential indoor yields around 400–500 grams per square meter under favorable conditions.

Plant structure can be influenced considerably by light intensity and vegetative time. Shorter vegetative growth and strong lighting favor more upright plants suitable for tighter spacing, while longer growth encourages additional branching. Mature flowers become substantial and resinous, and the larger leaves can create a dense canopy if plants are crowded. Adequate airflow is therefore important late in bloom, particularly around tightly packed flowers. Pistils begin cream-colored and gradually turn tan as maturity approaches, while the foliage and developing buds release increasingly strong pine-and-sweet aromatics.

Outdoor cultivation is less thoroughly documented than indoor production. Historical breeder descriptions placed harvest in October or November, indicating that Exile needs a reasonably long autumn to finish properly. Because Magus Genetics did not establish a dependable outdoor yield figure, precise gram-per-plant claims should be viewed skeptically. In a warm, dry climate with sufficient root space, the plant can develop substantial branching and flower mass, but late-season rain and humidity become increasingly relevant as dense buds mature. Overall difficulty is moderate: the cultivar is not exceptionally temperamental, yet canopy control, odor management, airflow and patience through its comparatively long indica flowering period all improve the chances of a quality harvest.
FAQ
Is Exile an indica or sativa?

Exile is an indica-dominant hybrid. Its original genetics combine 50% Warlock with 25% Northern Lights and 25% White Widow. Although Warlock and White Widow contribute some cerebral character, the finished plant was bred toward a stronger physical and sedating effect.
What are the genetics of the Exile strain?

The original Magus Genetics formula is Warlock × (Northern Lights × White Widow). Serious Seeds’ historical account confirms that Gerrit’s Warlock breeding stock was crossed with White Widow/Northern Lights to create Exile.
Who bred Exile?

Gerrit of Magus Genetics created the strain in the Netherlands. Serious Seeds later acquired much of the Magus collection, but the Exile mother had already been lost before the transfer, so the original variety is not part of Serious Seeds’ current preserved lineup.
What does Exile weed taste like?

The classic profile is sweet and strongly pine-forward, backed by earth, resin, subtle fruit and spice. Its aroma can be especially pungent while the plant is alive but becomes smoother and more rounded after drying and curing.
How long does Exile take to flower?

Indoor flowering generally lasts about 60–67 days, or approximately nine to ten weeks. Historical information places outdoor maturity between October and November, although climate can significantly change finishing time.
Final Thoughts on Exile

Exile is valuable today as much for its breeding history as for its effect. Warlock, Northern Lights and White Widow represent three foundational branches of modern marijuana genetics, and Magus Genetics brought them together without burying their identities beneath several generations of subsequent hybridization. The result was an unapologetically old-school cultivar: broad dark foliage, dense resinous flowers, intense sweet pine aroma and a heavy body-centered finish.

Its disappearance from the original breeder’s catalog gives the strain an additional layer of significance. When Serious Seeds incorporated the Magus Genetics collection, the mother plants needed to reproduce Exile authentically had already been lost. That makes today’s Exile name less straightforward than a currently stabilized seed variety and is exactly why accurate lineage information matters. For cannabis enthusiasts interested in pre-Cookies European breeding, classic indica effects or the history surrounding Warlock and Magus Genetics, Exile remains an unusually compelling piece of weed culture—even if finding an unquestionably authentic example has become far more difficult than it once was.
